chapter_title: Introduction to Ethereum: Beyond Bitcoin's Scope
chapter_summary:
While Bitcoin introduced the revolutionary concept of a decentralized digital currency, Ethereum took the underlying blockchain technology and expanded its potential far beyond simple value transfer. Imagine Bitcoin as a specialized calculator designed solely for secure transactions; Ethereum, in contrast, is a programmable world computer, capable of executing arbitrary code in a decentralized, trustless manner. This fundamental difference is what allows Ethereum to power a vast ecosystem of decentralized applications (DApps), financial instruments, and digital assets that go far beyond what Bitcoin was designed to do.

At the heart of Ethereum's programmability is the **Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)**. The EVM is a powerful, sandboxed virtual stack machine that executes code known as smart contracts. Every node in the Ethereum network runs an instance of the EVM, ensuring that all participants agree on the state of the blockchain and the outcome of contract executions. When a smart contract is deployed to Ethereum, its bytecode is stored on the blockchain. When a transaction calls a function within that contract, the EVM on every participating node executes that function, processes its logic, and updates the state of the contract accordingly. This deterministic execution environment is crucial for maintaining consensus across the decentralized network. It's important to understand that the EVM is completely isolated, meaning smart contracts cannot directly access network services, file systems, or other external processes outside the blockchain itself, enhancing security and predictability.

Ethereum operates with two distinct types of accounts, each serving a different purpose. An **Externally Owned Account (EOA)** is controlled by a private key, much like a Bitcoin wallet. These are the accounts that human users typically interact with, used for sending Ether, initiating transactions, and interacting with smart contracts. EOAs do not contain any code; they simply hold a balance of Ether and can sign transactions. In contrast, a **Contract Account** is controlled by the code stored within it. When a smart contract is deployed, a new contract account is created at a specific address, containing the contract's bytecode and its persistent storage. Unlike EOAs, contract accounts cannot initiate transactions on their own; they can only execute code when called by an EOA or another contract. This distinction is vital for understanding how interactions flow through the Ethereum network.

The native cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network is **Ether (ETH)**. While Ether can be traded as a digital asset, its primary utility within the Ethereum ecosystem is to pay for "gas." Gas is a unit of computational effort required to execute operations on the EVM. Every operation, from a simple addition to a complex smart contract function call, consumes a certain amount of gas. This mechanism serves several critical purposes: it prevents malicious actors from spamming the network with infinite loops or computationally expensive operations, compensates miners (or validators in Ethereum 2.0) for their computational resources, and prioritizes transactions based on the gas price users are willing to pay. Without gas, the "world computer" could easily be overwhelmed, making it unusable. Think of gas as the fuel that powers the EVM, where the price of fuel (gas price) and the amount of fuel needed (gas limit) determine the total transaction cost.

The overarching vision of Ethereum is to be a decentralized "world computer" – a global, open-source platform for decentralized applications. This means that applications built on Ethereum are not controlled by a single entity, are resistant to censorship, and can operate without intermediaries. From decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols to non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and supply chain tracking, Ethereum's programmable nature has unlocked an unprecedented wave of innovation. Understanding this foundational layer – the EVM, accounts, and the gas mechanism – is crucial for anyone looking to build, interact with, or simply comprehend the vast potential of the Ethereum blockchain.

screens.title: Introduction to Ethereum: Beyond Bitcoin's Scope
screens.subtitle: Why Ethereum is more than money — a programmable, decentralized runtime

narration.text: Today we'll orient around a single, central idea: Ethereum transforms the blockchain from a value-transfer ledger into a programmable, decentralized runtime. Think of Bitcoin as a specialist calculator designed to keep secure records of value. Ethereum is a world computer — a global platform that can run arbitrary programs called smart contracts. We'll look at the pieces that make that possible: the Ethereum Virtual Machine, the two account types you will encounter, and Ether's dual role as both currency and fuel. You will learn how the EVM enforces deterministic execution so every node reaches the same result, how externally owned accounts and contract accounts differ in who initiates actions, and why gas matters for security and resource allocation. As an example, imagine a vending machine implemented as a contract account: it has code and storage and performs fixed actions when triggered. A human user controls an externally owned account with a private key and initiates those interactions. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to explain why Ethereum enables decentralized applications that Bitcoin's design does not, and you'll be ready to explore account pages on a block explorer to see these roles in practice. Consider: what kinds of applications become possible when code itself is the authoritative agent on a shared ledger?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Ethereum is a programmable blockchain: a decentralized runtime (the EVM) that runs smart contracts, uses Ether to pay for computation, and relies on distinct account types to separate human control from code-controlled logic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to explain and do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives set a clear map for learning Ethereum's foundation. First, you'll distinguish Ethereum from Bitcoin by comparing purpose and functionality, so you can explain why Ethereum enables applications beyond simple value transfer. Second, you'll explain the Ethereum Virtual Machine: what deterministic execution means, why isolation matters, and how bytecode runs identically on every node. Third, you'll identify the two primary account types — Externally Owned Accounts and Contract Accounts — and describe how control flows between private keys and contract code. Fourth, you'll understand Ether's role as a cryptocurrency and as gas that pays for computation, including how gas prevents abuse and compensates nodes. Each objective combines a conceptual definition with a practical competency; for example, by the end you'll be able to open a block explorer and tell whether a page represents an EOA or a Contract Account. These skills matter because they let you reason about who initiates actions, how transactions consume resources, and how decentralized applications remain trust-minimized. As you move through the screens, look for the concrete examples and the small misconceptions we call out — they will help you solidify each objective into a verifiable competency.

narration.text: These applied objectives show you not just what to know but what to do. You will be able to read a block explorer page and identify whether an address is an EOA or a Contract Account by checking for code, read and interpret basic contract metadata stored on-chain, and explain the role of bytecode in contract accounts. You will also describe how gas limits and gas prices determine the total cost of a transaction and why that cost discourages infinite loops or spam. screens.title: Ethereum vs Bitcoin: Purpose and Scope
screens.subtitle: What changes when a ledger becomes programmable

narration.text: Start with a precise comparison. Bitcoin's design focuses on secure, decentralized value transfer: it records and protects ownership of digital currency. Ethereum builds on that ledger idea but adds programmability. That means rather than only storing balances, the network can store and execute code whose behavior is part of the canonical state. Concretely, Bitcoin is like a ledgered cash system — a reliable record of who owns what — whereas Ethereum is like a programmable machine where code defines behavior that the entire network enforces. For example, a token transfer on Bitcoin is limited to payment-like constructs. On Ethereum you can deploy a smart contract that implements a token, escrow rules, or a lending protocol that automatically enforces terms. A common misconception is to equate Ethereum simply with a cryptocurrency; while Ether is its currency, Ethereum's distinctive capability is the EVM that runs smart contracts deterministically. Another frequent misunderstanding is to assume contracts can access the web or local files: the EVM is isolated. Takeaway: think in terms of capability — Bitcoin secures value, Ethereum secures programmable state that can represent value plus logic. How would you design a simple escrow differently on each platform?

keyIdea.title: Difference in One Line
keyIdea.text: Bitcoin secures value; Ethereum secures programmable state, enabling decentralised applications and automated agreements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Ethereum vs Bitcoin
Side-by-side
Bitcoin — value transfer
Specialized ledger focused on secure currency transfers and balance history.
Ethereum — programmable state
Stores bytecode and executes smart contracts in a deterministic runtime shared by all nodes.
Concrete example
On Ethereum you can deploy an escrow contract that releases funds automatically when conditions are met. On Bitcoin similar functionality is more limited and not natively expressive the same way.
Common misconceptions
  • Ethereum is not just a currency; its core is the ability to run smart contract code.
  • Smart contracts are not autonomous agents with external access; they operate inside the EVM sandbox.
Key Takeaway

Programmability is the defining shift: Ethereum makes code part of the canonical state, enabling DApps and automated agreements.

screens.title: Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
screens.subtitle: A sandboxed, deterministic runtime every node runs

narration.text: The Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM, is the decentralized runtime that makes smart contracts possible. It is a sandboxed stack machine: every full node runs an instance of the EVM and executes the same contract bytecode so that all participants can agree on state changes. Deterministic execution is essential: given the same input and prior state, every EVM execution yields the same outcome. That determinism is how consensus can be maintained across a network of independent nodes. The sandboxing aspect means contracts cannot directly access external resources like the web or local files; this isolation improves security and predictability. In practice, a contract's Solidity source is compiled to bytecode that lives on-chain; when a transaction calls a function, each node runs that bytecode in its EVM. For example, calling a token transfer function will cause every node to execute the same opcodes, update balances, and record the new state. A misconception to avoid is believing contracts can spontaneously fetch off-chain data without an explicit mechanism; instead, external data must be introduced via transactions or oracle patterns. Takeaway: the EVM is the shared C P U that enforces identical behavior across the decentralized system.

keyIdea.title: EVM Insight
keyIdea.text: The EVM provides deterministic, sandboxed execution of smart contract bytecode, ensuring consistent state across all nodes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Ethereum Virtual Machine
EVM Architecture (high level)
Sandboxed runtime
Contracts run in isolation; no direct access to external networks or files.
Deterministic execution
Same bytecode + same input produces the same output on every node, enabling consensus.
Bytecode on-chain
Solidity compiles to bytecode stored with the contract account; that bytecode runs under the EVM.
Concrete example
Calling a transfer function runs the same sequence of opcodes on each node, which updates balances in the shared state. Nodes reach the same post-call state because execution is deterministic.
Why isolation matters
Isolation prevents contracts from producing non-deterministic effects caused by external systems. That containment keeps nodes in agreement and enhances security when code is replicated across the network.
Key Takeaway

EVM is the shared, isolated executor that ensures every node runs contract code the same way, enabling trustless, decentralized computation.

screens.title: Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs)
screens.subtitle: Human-controlled accounts that sign and initiate transactions

narration.text: An Externally Owned Account, or EOA, is the account type controlled by a private key. This is the entity users interact with when sending Ether or calling contracts. EOAs hold a balance of Ether and can sign transactions that instruct the network to move value or to invoke contract code. Crucially, EOAs do not contain code themselves; they are essentially key-controlled wallets. A useful concrete image is a person with a physical key unlocking a mailbox: the key allows them to initiate actions. A common misconception is to assume that because an EOA can call a contract it can force a contract to act at any time; contracts only run in response to transactions, either from EOAs or from other contracts. EOAs are the starting point for interactions: human intent is translated into a signed transaction, which then travels to nodes where the EVM executes any invoked contract code. When you inspect an EOA on a block explorer you will typically see a balance and a transaction history but no code or "Read/Write Contract" sections. Remember: EOAs initiate; contracts respond.

keyIdea.title: EOA Snapshot
keyIdea.text: EOAs are key-controlled accounts that sign transactions and hold Ether but do not contain executable code.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs)
Definition & Characteristics
  • Controlled by a private key.
  • Can sign and send transactions.
  • Holds Ether balance but contains no code.
  • Initiates interactions with contracts or transfers value.
Concrete example
A user with a wallet signs a transaction to call a contract's deposit function; that signed transaction originates from the EOA and triggers the contract's code when processed by nodes.
Block explorer cues
EOA pages show balance and transactions but lack a contract "Code" tab. Use that to distinguish human accounts from deployed contracts.
Key Takeaway

EOAs represent human-controlled keys that initiate on-chain actions; they are not stores of executable code.

screens.title: Contract Accounts and Smart Contracts
screens.subtitle: Code-controlled accounts that hold bytecode and storage

narration.text: Contract accounts are the ledger objects that represent deployed smart contracts. Unlike EOAs, contract accounts contain bytecode and persistent storage. When a smart contract is deployed, its bytecode is written to the blockchain at a specific address — that address is a contract account. Contract accounts cannot initiate transactions autonomously; they only execute in response to calls from EOAs or other contracts. Think of a smart contract like a vending machine: it sits at an address, holds state, and when a user inserts the correct input it executes pre-programmed logic. One practical implication is that you cannot sign from a contract; control flows through invocation. For example, a token contract stores balances and implements functions to transfer tokens; those functions execute only when called. Developers should not assume contract accounts can pull in off-chain data by themselves — external information must be supplied through transactions or via an oracle mechanism. On a block explorer a contract page usually shows code and "Read/Write" tabs to interact with the contract. Key takeaway: contracts are code at an address that respond to calls, maintain storage, and are limited by the EVM's sandbox.

keyIdea.title: Contract Account Snapshot
keyIdea.text: A contract account stores bytecode and persistent state and executes only when invoked by transactions from EOAs or other contracts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Contract Accounts
What a contract account holds
  • Bytecode compiled from a high-level language.
  • Persistent storage for variables, mappings, and balances.
  • An address that other accounts can call.
Concrete example
A token contract stores a mapping of balances and exposes transfer functions. When a user calls transfer, the contract's bytecode runs and updates storage across the network.
Explorer cues
Contract pages include a "Code" section and interactive "Read/Write Contract" panels, indicating deployed bytecode and callable functions.
Key Takeaway

Contract accounts are code-bearing addresses that react to calls and store state; they do not initiate transactions on their own.

screens.title: How Ether (ETH) and Gas Work
screens.subtitle: Gas as a metering unit and Ether as the fuel that pays for it

narration.text: Ether is the native asset of Ethereum, and while it can be traded like any cryptocurrency, its key on-chain utility is to pay for gas — the unit that measures computational effort. Every EVM operation consumes a predefined amount of gas. When you send a transaction, you specify a gas limit and a gas price; the total fee equals gas used times gas price, paid in Ether. This mechanism serves three purposes: it prevents denial-of-service by making excessive computation expensive, it compensates nodes for work, and it helps prioritize transactions by letting users offer higher gas prices. A simple example: a straightforward value transfer consumes a small amount of gas, while calling a complex contract function consumes more. A common misconception is to treat gas as separate currency — it's not; gas is paid in Ether. Also, setting an insufficient gas limit can cause a transaction to run out of gas, failing but still costing the gas spent. Remember: ether fuels computation, and gas is the meter that tracks how much fuel is consumed. Ask yourself: when designing a contract, how would you minimize gas usage for common operations?

keyIdea.title: Gas Principle
keyIdea.text: Gas measures computation; Ether pays for gas, which prevents abuse and compensates network participants.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Ether & Gas
Gas and fee components
Gas unit: a measurement of computational steps.
Gas limit: the maximum gas a transaction is allowed to consume.
Gas price: Ether amount offered per unit of gas.
Total fee: gas used multiplied by gas price, paid in Ether.
Concrete example
If a function costs 50,000 gas and the gas price is set to 20 units of Ether-denominated value per gas, the user pays Ether equivalent of 50,000 times that gas price. Insufficient gas limit causes failure but still consumes gas used so far.
Why gas exists
Gas prevents infinite loops and spam by attaching a cost to computation. It also aligns incentives by paying nodes for executing EVM operations.
Key Takeaway

Think of gas as the meter and Ether as the fuel. Together they make computation accountable and economically constrained.

screens.title: Gas Limit, Gas Price, and Transaction Outcomes
screens.subtitle: How choices affect cost, success, and resource use

narration.text: When you submit a transaction, you make two important choices: the gas limit and the gas price. The gas limit caps how much computation the transaction can consume. If execution exceeds that limit, the EVM halts and the transaction fails, but gas consumed up to that point is still spent. The gas price sets how much Ether you're willing to pay per unit of gas; higher gas prices can incentivize faster inclusion by validators. Together they determine the final Ether fee: gas used times gas price. This practical relationship matters for developers and users: contracts with expensive operations will require higher gas budgets, and callers must estimate costs or provide sufficient limits. A frequent misconception is that unused gas is always lost; in many implementations, leftover gas is refunded to the sender, but the precise refund rules depend on node and protocol specifics. From a design perspective, minimizing per-call gas consumption for common operations makes your contract cheaper to use. Guided question: when designing a frequently-used function, which code patterns would you avoid to reduce gas consumption and why? Gas Limit, Gas Price, and Transaction Outcomes means set a realistic gas limit and appropriate gas price: too low means failure, too high increases potential fees; optimize contract code to lower gas usage.. In practical terms, how choices affect cost, success, and resource use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical Rule
keyIdea.text: Set a realistic gas limit and appropriate gas price: too low means failure, too high increases potential fees; optimize contract code to lower gas usage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Gas Limit & Price
Transaction fee calculation
Gas used: actual units consumed by execution.
Gas limit: maximum allowed for the transaction.
Gas price: Ether-per-gas unit offered by the sender.
Total cost: gas used × gas price.
Concrete scenario
You call a contract expecting 100,000 gas usage and set a 120,000 gas limit. If code consumes 90,000 gas, you pay for gas used. If code unexpectedly consumes 130,000, execution halts and the transaction fails while still charging for gas consumed until failure.
Design guidance
Avoid expensive loops and unnecessary storage writes in frequently-called functions. Optimize for common paths to lower average cost for users.
Common mistake

Underestimating gas can cause failed transactions that still cost Ether. Always estimate conservatively and test on a testnet.

narration.text: Smart contracts start as high-level code and become bytecode that lives on-chain. A compiler translates the source into EVM bytecode, and deploying a contract writes that bytecode to a new contract account address. From then on, any call to that address triggers the EVM to run the same stored bytecode. This means the canonical behavior of a contract is defined by the bytecode on chain; the original source is convenience for humans. When you inspect a deployed contract you often see its bytecode, and sometimes a decompiled or verified source if the author published it. A concrete example: compiling a token contract produces initialization and runtime bytecode; the deploy transaction includes that initialization bytecode, which sets up storage and then leaves runtime bytecode behind at the contract address. Misconception check: the deployed contract does not retain the human-readable source by default; only bytecode and storage are guaranteed. For auditability, many projects publish source separately, but trust in behavior comes from the bytecode the EVM executes. Final question: why does storing behavior as bytecode on-chain improve decentralization and trust? Bytecode and Deployment means deploying a contract writes compiled bytecode to a contract account; that bytecode is the authoritative runtime the evm executes.. In practical terms, how source becomes on-chain behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deployment Fact
keyIdea.text: Deploying a contract writes compiled bytecode to a contract account; that bytecode is the authoritative runtime the EVM executes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Bytecode & Deployment
From source to on-chain bytecode
Step 1: Write contract source in a high-level language.
Step 2: Compile to EVM bytecode.
Step 3: Deploy bytecode in a transaction, creating a contract account with that runtime code.
Step 4: Calls to the address execute the stored bytecode across nodes.
Concrete example
A deploy transaction includes initialization bytecode that sets up storage. After deployment, the contract's runtime bytecode remains at the address and is what gets executed on subsequent calls.
Audit note
Bytecode is authoritative. Verified source is helpful for humans, but the EVM uses the stored bytecode to enforce behavior.
Key Takeaway

Deployment converts source to bytecode; that bytecode is what the EVM executes and what determines contract behavior on-chain.

screens.title: Transaction Flow: From EOA to State Change
screens.subtitle: How a signed intent becomes an on-chain state transition

narration.text: A typical transaction begins with an EOA signing a message that expresses intent, such as sending Ether or calling a contract function. That signed transaction is broadcast to the network and picked up by validators or miners, who include it in a block. When included, every full node executes the transaction's instructions in its EVM instance. If the transaction calls a contract, the EVM runs the contract's bytecode and applies the deterministic state changes, consuming gas as operations execute. If execution completes within the gas limit, the resulting state update is recorded; if it runs out of gas, the transaction fails while consuming gas used up to failure. An important distinction is that contract accounts cannot autonomously create transactions — they only react. This flow keeps a clear chain from human signature to consensus state: user intent, network propagation, deterministic execution, and finally persistent state changes. Misconception to correct: the EVM does not 'decide' to run code spontaneously; it only runs code in response to valid transactions. Closing question: how does this flow make smart contracts predictable and auditable? Transaction Flow: From EOA to State Change means eoa signs → broadcast to network → validators include it → evm executes bytecode → deterministic state update recorded, consuming gas.. In practical terms, how a signed intent becomes an on-chain state transition. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transaction Chain
keyIdea.text: EOA signs → broadcast to network → validators include it → EVM executes bytecode → deterministic state update recorded, consuming gas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Transaction Flow
Simplified transaction steps
  1. EOA signs a transaction expressing intent.
  2. Transaction is broadcast and included in a block by a validator/miner.
  3. Each node runs the transaction in the EVM, executing any contract bytecode.
  4. Deterministic state changes are recorded; gas is charged for work performed.
Concrete example
A user signs a call to a contract's withdraw function. Once included, nodes execute the same code which may update balances and storage according to the contract's logic, and the user pays gas for the computation.
Why predictability matters
Deterministic execution gives developers confidence that the same input will produce the same output everywhere, which is essential for audits and trustless applications.
Key Takeaway

Transactions transform signed user intent into deterministic, replicated state transitions via the EVM, with gas enforcing resource limits.

screens.title: Ethereum as a 'World Computer' and DApps
screens.subtitle: The vision: decentralized applications running without intermediaries

narration.text: Ethereum's long-term vision is often described as a "world computer": an open platform where decentralized applications run autonomously and resiliently without a single controlling party. In practice, DApps are built by deploying smart contracts that encode rules and state; users interact via EOAs that sign transactions. Because the EVM enforces the contract logic across many nodes, applications become resistant to single points of failure and censorship. Examples of DApps include decentralized finance protocols, token systems, and registries that manage assets without intermediaries. A common misconception is to assume 'decentralized' means no humans are involved; in reality, teams and communities still design, test, and upgrade contracts, but the runtime behavior of deployed contracts is enforced by the network. This architecture trades some developer convenience for the benefits of transparency and trust-minimization. Final reflection: when you design a DApp, which parts of your system should be on-chain to benefit from decentralization and which parts should remain off-chain for efficiency? Ethereum as a 'World Computer' and DApps means dapps are collections of smart contracts and off-chain interfaces that leverage the evm to run trust-minimized, censorship-resistant logic on a shared platform.. In practical terms, the vision: decentralized applications running without intermediaries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: World Computer
keyIdea.text: DApps are collections of smart contracts and off-chain interfaces that leverage the EVM to run trust-minimized, censorship-resistant logic on a shared platform.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › World Computer & DApps
What makes a DApp
  • One or more smart contracts holding logic and state.
  • Users interacting via EOAs that sign transactions.
  • Optional off-chain components for UI, indexing, or heavy computation.
Example categories
Decentralized finance, tokens and collectibles, supply chain registries — each uses on-chain contracts to enforce rules and state.
Design trade-offs
On-chain code gains decentralization and trustlessness but costs gas and must respect the EVM sandbox. Off-chain parts gain efficiency but require trust or additional mechanisms for verification.
Key Takeaway

Ethereum enables DApps by combining on-chain contracts for trust-minimized logic with off-chain components for performance and usability.

screens.title: Exploring EOAs and Contracts on a Block Explorer
screens.subtitle: A guided activity to observe the differences in practice

narration.text: This activity grounds ideas by observing real accounts. Start by finding a recent transaction and opening the sender's page. On an EOA you will see a balance and transaction history but no "Code" tab. Note the pattern of sending and receiving Ether and interactions with contracts. Next find a deployed contract address: its page will show a "Contract" section with "Code," "Read Contract," and possibly "Write Contract" interfaces. Inspect the code snapshot or bytecode and observe persistent state via read functions. The point is to see how contract accounts expose behavior and how EOAs simply hold keys and balances. A common pitfall is misreading contract proxies or multi-signature wallets as plain EOAs — focus on the presence of code to distinguish them. In your notes, record the differences you saw in balance patterns, available tabs, and whether the address initiated transactions. This direct observation reinforces the conceptual distinction and prepares you for designing interactions where an EOA triggers contract logic. Exploring EOAs and Contracts on a Block Explorer means use a block explorer to identify eoas by their lack of code and contract accounts by their code and read/write interfaces; record observed behavioral differences.. In practical terms, a guided activity to observe the differences in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Block Explorer Activity
Activity steps
  1. Find a recent transaction and open the "From" address page.
  2. Observe balance and transaction history for EOA cues.
  3. Search for a popular contract address and examine its "Code" and read/write sections.
  4. Compare and note differences in behavior and available interactions.
What to record
Note presence or absence of code, common transaction patterns, and whether the address initiates transactions. This helps solidify the EOA vs Contract Account distinction.
Key Takeaway

Hands-on inspection reinforces the conceptual differences: code presence, callable functions, and initiation patterns reveal account types.

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important concepts to remember. First, the Ethereum Virtual Machine is the decentralized runtime that executes smart contract bytecode deterministically and in a sandbox to keep nodes in agreement. Second, an Externally Owned Account is controlled by a private key, holds Ether, and initiates transactions; it does not contain executable code. Third, a Contract Account stores bytecode and persistent storage and executes only when invoked by transactions from EOAs or other contracts. These three ideas — the EVM, EOAs, and Contract Accounts — are the structural building blocks of Ethereum. Keep these compact mental models handy: the EVM is the shared C P U, EOAs are people with keys, and Contract Accounts are vending machines of code. Ask yourself which concept you'd explain first to a colleague who asks what makes Ethereum different from a simple cryptocurrency.

keyIdea.title: Memory Aid
keyIdea.text: EVM = shared CPU; EOA = human key; Contract Account = code at an address that reacts to calls.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Key Concepts
Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
The decentralized, sandboxed runtime that executes smart contracts deterministically.
Externally Owned Account (EOA)
A private key-controlled account used by humans to sign transactions; holds Ether but no code.
Contract Account
An address that stores bytecode and state; executes when called and cannot initiate transactions itself.
Summary
Keep these three building blocks in mind: the EVM executes bytecode, EOAs sign transactions, and Contract Accounts contain code and storage.

narration.text: Finish with the remaining essentials. Ether is the native cryptocurrency that also pays for gas. Gas is the unit of computation used to meter EVM operations, and paying gas in Ether prevents abuse and rewards participants. Smart contracts are self-executing code deployed as contract accounts that expose functions and maintain storage. Decentralized applications combine on-chain contracts with off-chain components to build services without centralized control. Keep in mind the practical consequences: gas creates an economic cost to computation, contract bytecode is authoritative, and EOAs remain the actors that initiate changes. Misconception to avoid: contracts do not magically access external data or run independently — they respond to transactions running inside the EVM. As you continue learning, use these compact reminders to reason about design choices: what to place on-chain, how gas shapes user experience, and why the EVM's sandboxing supports predictable consensus.

keyIdea.title: Final Reminder
keyIdea.text: Ether pays for gas; gas meters computation; contracts run only when called — these operational facts shape how DApps are designed and used.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Key Concepts
Ether (ETH)
Native asset used for value transfer and to pay for computation on the network.
Gas
Unit measuring computational effort; paying gas prevents abuse and compensates nodes.
Smart Contract / DApp
Self-executing code deployed on-chain that, combined with off-chain parts, forms decentralized applications.
Final takeaway
Remember these operational rules when building or interacting with Ethereum: who initiates, what pays for computation, and where logic runs.
